latin.251: GAR. Ultimo sic argumentatur. Mors spiritualis est mors metaphorice dicta; mors corporalis proprie. Quis autem existimet in lege, quae debuit verbis usitatissimis concipi, vocabulum unum, idemque debere accipi simul & proprie & metaphorice? praesertim cum morte mori figurato sensu, nescirem accipi, nisi forte Luc. IX. 60.
latin.252: PLAC. Vides, ut meam istam rationem contrahit, ut magna sui parte truncat, ut mihi tribuit, id quod non dixi, morte mori usurpari Luc. Ix. 60. Pergat tamen.
latin.253: GAR. Resp. Agnoscit Vir doctus, mortis nomine, tum mortem corporalem, tum etiam aeternum inferorum cruciatum intelligi, ut audivimus. Quid ergo responsurus est, si quis hoc argumentum ipsi reponat; vocem eandem in lege, quae debeat verbis usitatis concipi, non posse simul proprie & metaphorice sumi: cruciatum autem inferorum esse mortem metaphorice dictam, cum sola corporalis sit mors proprie dicta: ergo non posse his verbis intelligi cruciatum illum.
latin.254: PLAC. Ego vero respondebo, cum de foro Dei agitur nullam magis proprie mortem dici quam aeternam: a qua si corporalis sejungitur, ne mors quidem amplius vocari debet ipso Christo autore: Eam enim non comminatur lex, nisi quatenus est jactura omnium huius vitae bonorum. Jactura autem non est, cum in eorum locum succedunt meliora. Adde quod mors aeterna corporalem includit, id est, huius vitae privationem, ut illam: comminari lex non potuerit, quin istam simul comminaretur.
latin.255: GAR. 2. Cum Deus hic omnem mortem comminatus sit, qua dignum erat peccatum Adae, quidni dicamus & corporalem & spiritualem & aeternam fuisse comminatam, cum is omnibus subjacere mereatur peccator? PLAC. Omnis mors, qua dignum est peccatum, est mors diversa a peccato. Mors autem spiritualis est peccatum, & meretur mortem. GAR. 3. Nec vero Scripturis inusitatum est mortis nomine, mortem spiritualem designare, cum contrarium pateat, non modo ex Luc. 9. 60. Sed etiam ex frequentibus testimoniis, quorum etiam nonnulla jam produximus. PLAC. Non dixi inusitatum esse Scripturis nomen mortis pro morte spirituali: Dixi tantum inusitatum esse Scripturae veteris Testamenti, dixi toti Scripturae inusitatam esse phrasim, morte morieris eo sensu. Id ad meam istam rationem attineat. Jam laudaverat, nam ex Ezech. 3. 18. & ex Hos. 13. 1. sed frustra; nam ut ne ei opponam interpretes neutrum locum de morte spirituali accipientes, reclamat ipsa res. Agitur enim in illis locis de morte, quae non est omnium hominum communis, sed de morte in quam incurrunt quidam ob sua quaedam peccata actualia, cum mors spiritualis omnium sit hominum, & quidem ab ipso eorum ortu, antecedens omnia ipsorum actualia peccata. Itaque non possunt loca illa de spirituali morte, in privatione justitiae originalis sita, accipi.
latin.256: GAR. 4. Verbis usitatis, id est, vulgo notis leges concipi debere fatemur. Sed quis dicat verba metaphorica & impropria non esse usitata? Imo metaphoris nihil communius, etiam in legibus sanciendis, quae saepe una voce multa complectuntur, eaque diversissima, ut ad unius vocabuli proprietatem redigi non possint, sicuti patet in praeceptis Decalogi. PLAC. Dixine verba metaphorica, & impropria non esse usitata? Dixi tantum nomen mortis eo sensu metaphorico & improprio, quo significat mortem spiritualem, seu privationem justitiae originalis, non esse usitatum in vetere Testamento. Non negavi quin usurpentur interdum metaphorae in legibus, tantum negavi eas usurpari, quae sunt eo tempore, quo leges feruntur, inusitatae: negavi etiam eandem vocem in eadem lege semel usurpatam, simul & proprie & metaphorice intelligi debere. Tum enim demum accipi debet metaphorice, cum aliquid obest, quominus accipi possit aut debeat proprie. Neque propterea duplicem sensum Scripturae nego, literalem & mysticum: ille enim est verborum, hic potius rerum. In praeceptis Decalogi nullam vocem video, quae simul & proprie & improprie, seu metaphorice debeat exponi.

pass_a.251: GAR. Finally he argues thus. Spiritual death is death spoken metaphorically; corporal death properly. But who would think that in a law which ought to be conceived in most usual words, one and the same vocabulary-item ought to be taken at once both properly and metaphorically? especially since to die by death in a figured sense, I would not know to be taken, unless perhaps Luke 9:60.
pass_a.252: PLAC. You see how he contracts that reason of mine, how he truncates it in a great part of itself, how he attributes to me what I did not say, that to die by death is used in Luke 9:60. Let him go on nevertheless.
pass_a.253: GAR. Reply. The learned man acknowledges that by the name of death both corporal death and also the eternal torment of hell are understood, as we have heard. What then will he answer, if someone throws back this argument at him: that the same voice in a law which ought to be conceived in usual words cannot be taken at once properly and metaphorically: but that the torment of hell is death spoken metaphorically, since only corporal death is death properly so called: therefore that torment cannot be understood by these words.
pass_a.254: PLAC. But I will answer that when it is a matter of God's forum no death is more properly called death than eternal death: from which if corporal death is separated, it ought no longer even to be called death, by Christ himself as author: For the law does not threaten it except insofar as it is the loss of all goods of this life. But it is not a loss when better things succeed into their place. Add that eternal death includes the corporal, that is, the privation of this life, so that the law could not threaten that without at the same time threatening this.
pass_a.255: GAR. 2. Since God here threatened every death by which Adam's sin was worthy, why should we not say that corporal and spiritual and eternal were threatened, since the sinner deserves to be subject to all these? PLAC. Every death by which sin is worthy is a death diverse from sin. But spiritual death is sin, and merits death. GAR. 3. Nor indeed is it unused in the Scriptures to designate spiritual death by the name of death, since the contrary is plain, not only from Luke 9:60 but also from frequent testimonies, of which we have already produced some. PLAC. I did not say it is unused in the Scriptures for the name of death to stand for spiritual death: I said only that it is unused in the Scripture of the Old Testament; I said the phrase by death you shall die in that sense is unused to the whole Scripture. That belongs to that reason of mine. He had already praised, for from Ezek. 3:18 and from Hos. 13:1, but in vain; for even if I do not oppose to him interpreters taking neither place of spiritual death, the matter itself cries out. For in those places it is treated of a death which is not common to all men, but of a death into which certain ones incur for their certain actual sins, whereas spiritual death is of all men, and indeed from their very birth, preceding all their actual sins. Therefore those places cannot be taken of spiritual death situated in the privation of original righteousness.
pass_a.256: GAR. 4. That laws ought to be conceived in usual words, that is, commonly known, we confess. But who would say metaphorical and improper words are not usual? Indeed nothing is more common than metaphors, even in enacting laws, which often embrace many things in one voice, and those most diverse, so that they cannot be reduced to the propriety of one vocabulary-item, as is plain in the precepts of the Decalogue. PLAC. Did I say metaphorical and improper words are not usual? I said only that the name of death in that metaphorical and improper sense in which it signifies spiritual death, or the privation of original righteousness, is not usual in the Old Testament. I did not deny that metaphors are sometimes used in laws; I only denied that those are used which at the time when laws are made are unusual: I also denied that the same voice once used in the same law ought to be understood at once both properly and metaphorically. For then at last it ought to be taken metaphorically when something stands in the way so that it cannot or ought not to be taken properly. Nor do I on that account deny a double sense of Scripture, literal and mystical: for that is of the words, this rather of the things. In the precepts of the Decalogue I see no voice which ought to be expounded at once both properly and improperly, or metaphorically.

251: GAR. Finally he argues thus. Spiritual death is death said metaphorically; bodily death, properly. But who would think that in a law that had to be framed in the most ordinary words, one and the same term should be taken both properly and metaphorically at once—especially when I would not know 'to die the death' in a figured sense except perhaps at Luke 9:60?
252: PLAC. See how he shrinks that reason of mine, cuts away a large part of it, and credits me with what I never said—that 'to die the death' is used at Luke 9:60. Still, let him go on.
253: GAR. Reply. The learned man grants that 'death' covers both bodily death and the eternal torment of hell, as we have heard. What then will he say if someone turns his own argument back on him: the same word in a law that should use ordinary language cannot be taken properly and metaphorically together; hell's torment is death only metaphorically, since only bodily death is death properly so called; therefore those words cannot mean that torment.
254: PLAC. I answer: before God's court no death is more properly called death than eternal death. If you split bodily death off from it, even that no longer deserves the name 'death,' by Christ's own teaching. The law threatens eternal death only as the loss of all this life's goods—and that is no loss when better goods take their place. Add that eternal death includes the bodily—the loss of this life—so the law could not threaten the one without also threatening the other.
255: GAR. 2. Since God here threatened every death Adam's sin deserved, why not say he threatened bodily, spiritual, and eternal death, when the sinner deserves to lie under them all?
PLAC. Every death that sin deserves is a death other than sin. Spiritual death is itself sin, and it merits death.
GAR. 3. Nor is it unusual in Scripture to call spiritual death by the name 'death'; the opposite is clear not only from Luke 9:60 but from many other texts we have already cited.

PLAC. I did not say Scripture never uses 'death' for spiritual death. I said only that that sense is unused in the Old Testament, and that the phrase 'you shall die the death' in that sense is unused in Scripture as a whole. That is what my reason needs. He had already appealed to Ezek. 3:18 and Hos. 13:1—but in vain. Even without opposing interpreters who take neither place of spiritual death, the subject itself objects: those texts treat a death not common to all, but a death some incur for particular actual sins, whereas spiritual death belongs to all from birth and precedes every actual sin. So those places cannot mean spiritual death as the privation of original righteousness.
256: GAR. 4. We grant that laws should be framed in ordinary, commonly known words. But who says metaphorical or improper words are not ordinary? Metaphors are nowhere more common than in framing laws, which often pack many and very different things into one word that cannot be reduced to a single proper sense—as the Decalogue's precepts show.

PLAC. Did I say metaphorical and improper words are unused? I said only that 'death' in the metaphorical, improper sense that means spiritual death—or the privation of original righteousness—is unused in the Old Testament. I never denied that laws sometimes use metaphors; I denied using metaphors that were unusual when the laws were made, and I denied that the same word, used once in the same law, must be read both properly and metaphorically at once. Metaphor comes in only when something blocks taking the word properly. That does not make me deny Scripture's double sense, literal and mystical: the first belongs to the words, the second rather to the things. In the Decalogue I see no word that must be read both properly and improperly—or metaphorically—together.
